english: A subset $X$ of $\{1,2,3,\dots,10\}$ is chosen at random, all $2^{10}$ subsets being equally likely. The probability that each of the three sets $X\cap\{1,2,3\}$, $X\cap\{3,4,5\}$ and $X\cap\{5,6,7\}$ is non-empty is
hindi: समुच्चय $\{1,2,3,\dots,10\}$ का एक उपसमुच्चय $X$ यादृच्छया चुना जाता है, सभी $2^{10}$ उपसमुच्चय समसम्भाव्य हैं। तीनों समुच्चयों $X\cap\{1,2,3\}$, $X\cap\{3,4,5\}$ तथा $X\cap\{5,6,7\}$ में से प्रत्येक के अरिक्त होने की प्रायिकता है
solution: Each element is in $X$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, independently; $P(X$ misses a given set of $k$ elements$)=2^{-k}$
solution_full: Since all $2^{10}$ subsets are equally likely, each element of $\{1,\dots,10\}$ belongs to $X$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, independently of the others. Hence $X$ misses a fixed set of $k$ elements with probability $\dfrac{2^{10-k}}{2^{10}}=2^{-k}$. Elements $8,9,10$ play no role.

Complement: let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be the events that $X$ contains no element of $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{3,4,5\}$, $\{5,6,7\}$ respectively. The required event is the complement of 'at least one of $A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}$ occurs'.
Single events: each set has $3$ elements, so $P(A_{1})=P(A_{2})=P(A_{3})=\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Pairs: $A_{1}\cap A_{2}$ means $X$ misses $\{1,2,3\}\cup\{3,4,5\}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ (5 elements, because the sets share 3), probability $\dfrac{1}{32}$. Similarly $P(A_{2}\cap A_{3})=\dfrac{1}{32}$. But $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{5,6,7\}$ are disjoint, so $A_{1}\cap A_{3}$ means missing 6 elements: probability $\dfrac{1}{64}$.
Addition theorem for three events: $P(A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup A_{3})=\dfrac{3}{8}-\dfrac{1}{32}-\dfrac{1}{32}-\dfrac{1}{64}+\dfrac{1}{128}=\dfrac{48-4-4-2+1}{128}=\dfrac{39}{128}$.

Hence the required probability is $1-\dfrac{39}{128}=\dfrac{89}{128}$. (Treating the three conditions as independent would give $\left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{343}{512}$, which is wrong because the sets overlap.)
originality_note: New: a random subset required to hit three overlapping blocks, so the pairwise intersections of the complementary events have unequal probabilities (shared element versus disjoint blocks) and inclusion-exclusion has to track the overlap structure (way 5: complement, addition theorem for three events and inclusion-exclusion linked). Closest known: 'probability that a number is divisible by 2, 3 or 5' and random-subset hitting problems in research papers. Different because: the unequal pair terms 1/32, 1/32, 1/64 come from the geometry of the blocks, not from given data.

concept_use.Probability using the principle of inclu: The three intersection terms have different sizes and are combined by inclusion-exclusion over the missed blocks.
concept_use.Complementary events and 'at least one': The required 'every block is hit' event is the complement of 'at least one block is missed'.
